cards.b:
Microbes outnumber all other life. They cause diseases, but they also make curd, medicines, oxygen and soil fertility. You carry about as many bacterial cells as human ones. This lesson shows who they are.

A single teaspoon of soil can hold billions of bacteria. They were Earth's first life, perhaps 3.5 billion years ago, and bacteria such as cyanobacteria created the oxygen in our air. In your gut they digest fibre and train your immune system. The microbial world includes bacteria, archaea, protists, fungi and viruses, which differ greatly in structure. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first saw bacteria with a homemade microscope around 1676, calling them 'animalcules'.

Bacteria: single prokaryotic cells with a cell wall. Viruses: genetic material in a protein coat, not cells. Fungi: eukaryotes with chitin walls, such as yeast, moulds and mushrooms. Archaea and protists add to the mix.

Shapes: rods (bacilli), spheres (cocci), spirals. They reproduce by dividing every 20 minutes in good conditions, swap genes through plasmids (conjugation) and may form tough spores. Gram staining (Hans Christian Gram, 1884) separates two wall types. Helpful: Lactobacillus (curd), Rhizobium (fixes nitrogen), gut flora. Harmful: cholera, TB, typhoid.

A virus lands on a host cell, injects its genes, makes the cell build more viruses, and bursts out or buds off. Bacteriophages attack bacteria. Examples: influenza, HIV, SARS-CoV-2, rabies, dengue. Dmitri Ivanovsky (1892) and Beijerinck (1898) first showed tobacco mosaic disease is caused by something smaller than bacteria.

Yeast (single cell) makes bread rise and brews alcohol. Moulds make penicillin: Alexander Fleming noticed Penicillium killing bacteria in 1928; Florey and Chain made it a drug in the 1940s (Nobel 1945). Fungi also cause athlete's foot, ringworm and, in weak patients, serious infections. Many form partnerships with roots (mycorrhiza) or algae (lichens).

Antibiotics kill or stop bacteria, not viruses. If a few bacteria survive, they multiply and pass on resistance. Misuse speeds this. 'Superbugs' resist many drugs.

Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould, Penicillium, killed bacteria around it, and Howard Florey and Ernst Chain made it into a drug in the 1940s. Different antibiotics attack different weak points: penicillin blocks cell wall building, which human cells do not have, so it harms bacteria but not us. Resistance arises by chance mutations and gene swapping. To slow it, finish the doctor's course, never use leftovers, and do not demand antibiotics for colds. Antimicrobial resistance is a serious problem in India.

Pasteur and Robert Koch proved germs cause disease in the 1860s-80s. Koch found the TB bacillus in 1882 and the cholera bacillus in 1883. Koch's postulates set the test. Joseph Lister (1867) used antiseptics. Electron microscopy first pictured viruses in the 1930s.

Before germ theory, people blamed 'bad air' (miasma). Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation with his swan-neck flasks in 1859-61, and showed that heating (pasteurisation) kills microbes in milk. Koch's postulates: the germ must be found in every case, grown in pure culture, cause the disease when put in a healthy host, and be recovered again. Not every disease fits these rules, but they changed medicine. Lister's carbolic acid spray reduced surgical deaths sharply. John Snow traced cholera in London to a water pump in 1854.

Fix these

  • Most bacteria are harmless or helpful.
  • Antibiotics do not treat colds or flu.
  • Viruses are not killed by antibiotics because they have no cell machinery to target.

Also, 'germs' include more than bacteria: viruses cause flu and measles, fungi cause ringworm and athlete's foot, and protists cause malaria. Washing hands with soap works by breaking the oily coat of many germs and lifting them off, and is among the most effective ways to prevent infection.

Also, 'germs' include more than bacteria: viruses cause flu and measles, fungi cause ringworm and athlete's foot, and protists cause malaria. Washing hands with soap works by breaking the oily coat of many germs and lifting them off the skin, and is among the most effective ways to prevent infection. Sterilising and boiling water work by killing microbes with heat.

Waldemar Haffkine, working in Mumbai in 1897, developed an early plague vaccine and a cholera vaccine. S.N. De at Kolkata (1959) showed that cholera toxin causes the disease. Indian curd, idli and dosa depend on microbes. Biogas and biofertilisers (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, blue-green algae) support farmers. India's national action plan on antimicrobial resistance began in 2017.

• Bacteria are cells; viruses are not; fungi have chitin walls.
  • Viruses hijack host cells.
  • Antibiotics fight bacteria; misuse causes resistance.
  • Fleming found penicillin in 1928.

Think about it:

  1. Why is a course of antibiotics usually completed?
  2. Why is a virus harder to treat than bacteria?
